[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When light or heavy emphatic nūn follows a singular jussive verb, its final consonant takes fatḥa; kasra or ḍamma would confuse gender or number.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A singular indicative verb takes fatḥa before emphatic nūn so it is not confused with the plural form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a dual indicative verb, heavy nūn replaces the dual nūn but leaves the alif, preserving the dual marker; light nūn cannot follow the alif because it is not assimilated.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When emphatic nūn is added to an indicative plural verb, the indicative nūn is deleted, avoiding a sequence of three nūns or disliked doubling.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض القراء وأهل المدينة | reports | Some readers read أتحاجوني, and the Medinans read فبم تبشرون, reducing doubled nūn because they found gemination heavy. | mentions 15:54

[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unvocalized feminine singular yāʾ is dropped before emphatic nūn to avoid adjacent sukūns; in indicative forms the indicative nūn drops and the yāʾ remains.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For a masculine plural, the indicative nūn drops before emphatic nūn and the wāw remains, as it does in the imperative.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابأحوالالحروفالتيقبلالنونالخفيفةوالثقيلة)#641/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the attached pronoun marker would meet a following hamzat al-waṣl or article, it is vocalized to prevent two sukūns, with the same vowel used before emphatic nūn.

[FARISI-HUJJA:v3p332/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Arabic also resolves repeated sounds by deletion or substitution; poetry and Sībawayh's report of a reader support deleting the second nūn, a dialect attributed by some Basrans to Ghatafan.
